newsitem.title: USA: NYC mayor says overtime pay rose more modestly.
newsitem.headline: NYC mayor says overtime pay rose more modestly.

text.p: The amount of overtime paid to New York City workers rose, though more modestly than in the past, while absenteeism declined, according to a semi-annual "report card" Mayor Rudolph Giuliani issued on Thursday.

The Republican mayor focused on the city's continuing drop in crime, saying it was ahead of any other city in the country, as he presented a detailed study that has been required twice a year from every mayor since 1977.
The report covered the first four months of fiscal year 1997, which began July 1. It said that the employee absence rate fell from 3.82 percent to 3.64 percent when measured against a year-ago.
Total overtime pay increased 11 percent to $18.2 million, though this was a much smaller increase than the $159.3 million jump seen in the year-ago period.

The city's difficulty controlling overtime pay has raised questions, though it says much of the spending was due to anti-drug efforts, that have forced prison guards to work longer hours as they cope with a rising number of people who are arrested.
In the latest report, the Fire Department also accounted for much of the rise in overtime.

The welfare caseload continued to drop, going from a little over one milion a year ago to 971,400. There were slight increases in the number of homeless families and individuals being housed by the city, despite its improving economy.

Parks and streets were rated as cleaner, and Giuliani took the opportunity to praise a controversial workfare program, which advocates for the poor and unions have criticized. The program obliges people on welfare to work in various city departments, including sanitation, to get benefits.
The mayor also pointed out that the federal welfare laws approved last August impose work requirements.

Saying it was fortunate that the city had its big workfare plans, Giuliani said: "I just ask you to consider the condition the city would be in now, having to face mandates from the federal government."
The mayor added that one of the keys to the drop in crime has been falling reports of shooting incidents, a closely watched measure.

During the first four months of fiscal 1997, there were 860 such incidents, down sharply from 1,221 a year-ago. And when measured against the 1995 fiscal period, the achievement is even more dramatic, as there were 1,600 such incidents then--twice the latest level.
A total of 56 percent of the city's highway miles have been "adopted" by private companies or individuals, who have taken on the burden of keeping them clean.
The mayor, who has said that litter-strewn highways give tourists a bad impression of the city, added this was an increase from 35 percent last year.
